q.intro.text: A cone-shaped paper cup and a can have the same radius, four inches, and the same height, six inches.

q.ask.text: You fill the cup with water and pour it into the can, again and again. How many full cups fill the can?

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the picture moves first, then the notation.

e.s1.text: One layer is the base circle: pi times three squared, nine pi square inches. The can is five inches of layers: nine pi times five is forty-five pi cubic inches.

e.s2.text: Three full cones fill the can exactly. So one cone holds a third of it: forty-five pi divided by three is fifteen pi cubic inches.

e.s3.text: A ball with radius three inches is six inches tall, so its can is six inches tall: nine pi times six is fifty-four pi. The ball’s water fills two thirds of it: thirty-six pi cubic inches.

e.s4.text: It works for any size. Cylinder: pi r squared h. Cone: one third pi r squared h. Sphere: two thirds of pi r squared times two r, which is four thirds pi r cubed.

e.why.text: Quick check. Why was the ball’s can six inches tall, not five?

e.w-ok.text: Yes. The can that just holds a ball is as tall as the ball, and a ball is as tall as its diameter: two radii.

e.w-any.text: A taller can holds more, so the ball would fill less than two thirds of it. The two thirds is for the can exactly as tall as the ball.

e.w-half.text: The ball fills two thirds of its can, not half. The six inches is the ball’s own height, its diameter.

t.intro.text: A snow-cone cup has radius two inches and height six inches, and so does its can. The first two steps are done for you.

t.s1.text: Layers: pi times two squared is four pi square inches, times six inches. The can holds twenty-four pi cubic inches.

t.s2.text: The cup is a third of it: twenty-four pi divided by three is eight pi cubic inches.

t.h.text: Now a gumball with radius two inches. How tall is the can that just holds it?

t.h-ok.text: Yes, four inches. The gumball is as tall as its diameter, two plus two.

t.h-six.text: Six inches was the cup’s can. This can only has to be as tall as the gumball.

t.h-r.text: Two inches reaches only to the gumball’s middle. It is as tall as its diameter.

t.h-no.text: The can is exactly as tall as the gumball. How tall is a ball with radius two inches?

t.v.text: Its can holds pi times two squared times four, sixteen pi cubic inches. How much does the gumball hold, exactly?

t.v-ok.text: Yes. Two thirds of sixteen pi is thirty-two thirds pi cubic inches, about thirty-three and a half.

t.v-half.text: Half of the can would be eight pi. Watch the pour: a ball fills two thirds of its can.

t.v-can.text: Sixteen pi is the whole can. The ball leaves room in the corners: it fills two thirds.

t.v-third.text: One third is the cone. The ball fills two thirds of its can.

t.v-no.text: Take two thirds of sixteen: multiply by two, divide by three. A fraction is fine.

t.cb-right.text: At the start you picked three cups, and you were right. Now you can show why: a cone is one third of its matching cylinder.

t.cb-half.text: At the start you picked two cups. A cone looks like half a can, but the pour shows it: three cups fill it.

t.cb-four.text: At the start you picked four cups. The pour shows it takes exactly three.

p.intro.text: Jordan says: my cone vase has radius three inches and height ten inches. A can with radius three inches and height five inches holds forty-five pi cubic inches. A cone is a third of a cylinder, so my vase holds fifteen pi cubic inches. Is Jordan right?

p.test.text: Let’s test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.prove.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: Jordan’s can is not the vase’s match,

p.c2.text: The vase’s own cylinder holds nine pi times ten, ninety pi cubic inches,

p.c3.text: So the vase holds thirty pi cubic inches, twice Jordan’s answer,

p.ok1.text: Right. The vase is twice as tall as the can, so the can is not its match.

p.ok2.text: Right. Same base, nine pi, stacked ten inches high.

p.x-any.text: That is exactly Jordan’s slip. The one third only works for the cylinder with the same base and the same height.

p.x-half.text: A cone fills one third of its cylinder, not half. Three cones fill it.

p.x-twice.text: The one third is used once, on the cone’s own cylinder. Dividing again makes it far too small.

p.x-other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That’s a proof: three claims, each with its reason, and the pour backs the last one. Jordan used a cylinder that was not the cone’s match.
